波场到底谁说了算？把java-tron、DPoS和TVM拆开看

波场的去中心化，到底去中心化在哪里？待我娓娓道来

1 / 规则写在代码里

波场的核心客户端是开源的 java-tron，交易处理、区块验证、共识、账户状态、资源计算等，都在客户端里。

if (verifyTransaction(tx)
    && verifyBlock(block)
    && verifyState(state)) {
    accept(); }

实际源码当然比这复杂得多，简单理解就是，不是超级代表说这个区块有效，它就有效，而是其他节点按照同一套规则重新验证。

这也是我理解波场去中心化的第一层，规则先于参与者。

2 / 27个超级代表负责出块

波场采用DPoS，用户质押TRX获得TRON Power，再投票给超级代表候选人，排名前27的成为活跃超级代表，负责轮流生产区块。

TRX质押 - 获得投票权 - 选出超级代表 - 超级代表出块 - 其他节点验证

如果某个超级代表出问题，其他节点不会跟着接受错误区块。

3 / 一笔交易怎么进入区块？

签名 → 验证 → 打包 → 广播 → 再验证 → 确认

所以“3秒出块”和最终确认并不是一回事。3秒代表交易可以很快进入区块，后续随着更多超级代表继续出块，区块进入固化状态。

4 / TVM负责智能合约

智能合约运行在TVM，它最重要的一个特点就是确定性。

相同代码
+ 相同输入
+ 相同链上状态
= 相同执行结果

节点按照同样的规则执行合约，结果一致，状态才能被写入账本。这也是为什么超级代表虽然负责出块，却不能随意修改智能合约执行结果。 
最来说下，所以认为波场的去中心化，核心并不是“谁来管理”，而是没有谁可以脱离规则单独决定结果。

代码、节点、选票和共识，共同把这套网络撑起来。

苹果将限制 AI 随意访问 Mac 磁盘

10月2日，苹果宣布收紧Mac的"完全磁盘访问权限"，以后任何应用想拿这个权限，必须经过"非常明确的用户操作"许可。

苹果表示，"随着AI Agent越来越强大、越来越自主，这种级别访问带来的风险将大幅增长。"

Agent能读走你整台Mac，包括邮件、短信、浏览记录、备份… 一个不落

公告大意：

苹果为开发者提供功能强大的 API，同时通过隐私控制措施保护用户的数据。“完全磁盘访问”会绕过其中很大一部分限制，让 Mac 上的备份软件能够正常工作。

但一些开发者对这项权限的使用方式，可能让用户在没有充分知情和理解的情况下，暴露文件、邮件、消息乃至浏览记录。对于通信应用，这还可能影响与用户交流的其他人的隐私。

苹果计划增加控制措施，确保用户只有经过非常明确的主动操作，才能授予应用如此广泛的访问权限。

苹果认为，随着 AI 智能体的能力和自主性不断增强，这种权限带来的风险会显著上升。因此，用户需要在授权之前清楚理解风险，才能对自己的数据和隐私作出知情选择。
原文：https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=p6zjojqw

Doing a bit of a self-experiment.

Goal: use my personal health and travel data to provide personalized diet and exercise recommendations for me, using frontier models but in a way that avoids leaking to them any private information.

Strategy: use a local model (Qwen 3.8 Flash Next) to orchestrate, and use powerful remote models as a tool call to benefit from higher-level thinking and knowledge that the local model does not have.

Three-layer approach to privacy:

Avoid leaking personally identifiable information, or leaking my identity through writing style -> local model writes the queries to the frontier model, not me
Avoid leaking who I am through the payment channel -> zkAPI
Avoid leaking who I am through networking / IP -> Tor

You need all three (and finally we have all three, at least to some extent)

A skill file teaches the local model when and how to construct minimally-data-revealing requests to remote models. Use zkAPI-wrapped-with-Tor as a CLI tool.

And everything works! I got the recommendations back, info from frontier models helped to improve them.

Main deficiencies:

* Tor is really not optimized for request-by-request de-linking, which is the only form of network-layer privacy that really makes sense in today's world (long-running identifiers are too fragile). Probably not private enough, and latency 10-100x higher than it could be, at the same time.
* The skill file's request construction strategies are definitely far from optimal.
* Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is still too slow for comfort. It's comfortably running at 20-30 TPS, but it would only really start to feel fast at 100+
* There is a tradeoff: the more careful you are about what data you give to a remote model, the less it can help you

dots is 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗳𝗮𝘃𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 right now. Over the past few days it's become my main one. Especially when it's open on my desktop and talking to it feels like talking to a real person, it feels incredibly futuristic.

I care a lot about how things feel. For some reason, the dots interface looks a lot like iMessage, and it's unusually smooth to use. The web app used to have a bug where dragging the sidebar edge overlapped the chat box in the bottom right. No big deal.

Besides texting it, I also just call it. I've kept my GPT subscription partly for GPT Live's voice. I still haven't found anything that matches its latency and how human it feels. Some people say dots calls are just GPT Live with a different entry point. In my experience, connecting takes a bit longer, but once you're connected it's a lot steadier, and it answers fast. And whether I'm texting or calling, on my phone or my computer, it's the same dot, hooked up to most of my plugins, including the ones I wrote myself.

Since it's this much like a coworker, it should get a workbench too. I've found Space works especially well with dots: give it a Space of its own, it updates its progress there, you edit right on the page, and when something needs doing, you @ it. Working together feels just like working with a real person, only much faster. Add a few scheduled tasks so it checks on its own at set times and updates the page itself. It's insanely good.

Over these past few days, a lot of different writing and content work has all come together through it. My guess is that's why OpenAI built dots and put it second in the left sidebar. It may end up as ChatGPT's front door.

Right now, chatting with your dot 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗚𝗣𝗧 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘀. Tasks it hands off to Codex or ChatGPT Work still count toward those products' limits as usual, and for the first month after launch, its allowance for heavier work is extended. Make the most of it and set up a workbench for your dot: create a new Space, name it "Workbench," then send it this 👇

"I created a Space called Workbench. You'll maintain it from now on. Put three pages in it:
- In progress: everything I'm following up on, with its status, next step, and who it's waiting on
- Needs my decision: decisions I need to make, with the options and your recommendation
- Today: what you did today and which page you changed, with each new day at the top
Every weekday at 9 a.m. (my time zone), check the email, Slack and calendar I've connected (skip any I haven't), and update these three pages when something changes. You can handle research, organizing and updating these pages on your own. Before replying to emails, sending messages or editing other people's documents, ask me first. If a deadline is at risk or something needs my decision, message me in ChatGPT. When I @ you on a page, make the changes my comment asks for.
After you set up the scheduled task, tell me where it's saved and when it runs, then do a test run. If you can't set it up, tell me straight away."

quoted_tweet.author: Rothmus 🏴
quoted_tweet.text:
A humanoid is a capital good on a scale that changes the constraint. It lengthens production and raises what labor and land can turn out, which is the abundance Elon is pointing at.

A person supplies about 2,000 hours a year. A robot on a 168 hour week supplies about 8,700. His floor of 1 billion within 10 years, priced in the low 10,000s, equals about 4 billion full time equivalents against a world labor force of 3.5 billion. 
The 10 billion at 15 years is an order of magnitude past that. 

Robots building robots still require saving, because energy, materials, and machines have to be bid into that line.
Expected abundance holds for ordinary wants which is what matters for people as consumers. Housing, food, care, and routine medicine get repriced toward energy and materials until a household’s budget stops being what limits them. 

An owner running 100s or 1,000s of agents earns the return on that capital stock, which is also how universal high income shows up as purchasing power. 

Money prices remain the way to allocate whatever is still scarce, that is energy, locations, raw materials. At least in the short term. 

Energy is the binding input, and settling more than one planet adds land, minerals, and generation beyond a single world.

TLDR: (1) More energy. (2) Multiplanetary doesn’t hurt.

Startup Idea: Make a platform that hosts video games and makes them multiplayer. 

Don't build an agent that builds video games. 
Waste of time. 

Build an agent native app that allows me to go to your site, copy a link, paste it into codex, claude or grok and say... "Please make this game multiplayer so i can play it with my friends"

And their agent will look at your docs and efficiently host and list the game on your platform. 

Any type of game, just get the little things right like real time db, latency, and any other small details that make the games more fun. 

Have a little friction as possible. And make it free. 

After you get enough people on the platform implement a GAMEBUCKS... or something and let people add purchases to their games, and take a cut of that. 

You'll find ways to monetize. 

But only do games, and make the games on the platform discoverable.
